contributions.headingText: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant glandular neoplasm involving endocervix.

2C77.1 Adenocarcinoma of cervix uteri

2C77.Y Other specified malignant neoplasms of cervix uteri
Acceptable: endometrioid adenocarcinoma of endocervix; endometrioid adenocarcinoma secondarily involving cervix; serous carcinoma secondarily involving cervix; adenocarcinoma NOS

There is no information about primary endometrioid adenocarcinoma or adenocarcinoma NOS. Carcinomas secondarily involving the cervix may be associated with vaginal bleeding, nonspecific pelvic symptoms, elevated serum CA125 levels, and/or positive Pap tests. The primary site usually displays a dominant mass.

Endometrioid adenocarcinoma is rare, accounting for no more than 1% of all primary endocervical adenocarcinomas {29135516}, whereas endometrioid adenocarcinoma of endometrium invades the cervical stroma in approximately 10% of cases {30238246}. Because of morphological similarities to usual-type adenocarcinoma and a lack of proper definitions, the reported prevalence was higher in older publications {12207781; 11002225}. Despite studies of primary cervical serous carcinoma in the older literature {9422324}, there is now a general consensus that most or all serous carcinomas detected in the cervix represent metastasis or direct extension from adnexal or endometrial serous carcinomas {20414103}, although conclusive studies to support this have not yet been published. Nearly all endocervical adenocarcinomas (98%) can be subclassified into HPV-associated and HPV-independent types using H&E-stained sections on the basis of the recommendations of the International Endocervical Adenocarcinoma Criteria and Classification (IECC) {29135516; 29877920}, meaning that the NOS category should be used only rarely. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Endometrioid adenocarcinoma of endocervix is thought to arise in endometriosis. Endometrioid adenocarcinoma secondarily involving cervix extends directly (involving mucosa and/or stroma) or indirectly (involving mucosa by lymphovascular invasion) from the uterine corpus and lower uterine segment. These tumours are frequently intermediate/high-grade and deeply invasive into myometrium with prominent lymphovascular invasion {23063759}. Serous carcinoma secondarily involving cervix extends directly (involving mucosa and/or stroma) from corpus and lower uterine segment or indirectly (involving mucosa by implantation or lymphovascular invasion). Adenocarcinoma NOS is a heterogeneous category.
Tumours of endometrioid subtype usually present as a visible polypoid or ulcerated cervical mass.

The endometrioid subtype must present confirmatory endometrioid features: at least focal low-grade endometrioid glands lined by columnar cells with light eosinophilic cytoplasm and pseudostratified bland nuclei, with or without squamous differentiation and/or cervical endometriosis. Therefore, cervical endometrioid carcinomas must have an appearance that is identical to that of endometrioid carcinomas in the endometrium. The one possible exception is stromal invasion by highly differentiated endometrioid glands without a stromal response {8317607}. A 2003 publication on the topic describes the same not-infrequent pattern of endometrioid endometrial carcinoma that secondarily involves cervix {12883240}. Unlike HPV-associated adenocarcinomas, endometrioid carcinomas do not display apical mitoses and apoptotic bodies at scanning magnification. p16 may be block-positive in high-grade lesions; however, most endometrioid adenocarcinomas show patchy positivity for p16, and all are negative for HPV. True endometrioid adenocarcinoma of endocervix should not be reflexively diagnosed in the presence of a mucin-poor endocervical adenocarcinoma, even when cribriform architecture is present. This diagnosis can only be established after a primary endometrial carcinoma and HPV infection are excluded.

Serous carcinoma secondarily involving cervix is morphologically identical to serous and high-grade serous carcinomas that arise elsewhere. A Pap test, endocervical curettage, or biopsy reporting serous carcinoma is not sufficient for a primary serous carcinoma diagnosis. An aberrant p53 staining pattern without HPV infection must be present in any putative primary cervical serous carcinoma, and primary serous carcinomas of endometrium and adnexa must be excluded.

The morphology of endocervical adenocarcinoma NOS is obscure, but pathologists are strongly encouraged to classify these tumours on the basis of the presence of HPV. HPV-associated adenocarcinomas, as discussed in other chapters, show obvious floating mitoses and karyorrhexis. Ancillary testing for the presence of HPV may require a specific assay (mRNA-based high-risk HPV in situ hybridization) or an indirect assay (p16 immunohistochemistry). The pitfalls of these methods are discussed in the section on HPV-associated endocervical adenocarcinoma (see section Adenocarcinoma, HPV-associated, of the uterine cervix). HPV-independent adenocarcinomas usually have characteristic histological appearances, but subclassification may be difficult in small samples. A limited panel of immunohistochemical stains (p16, ER, and GATA3) can be used to narrow the differential diagnosis {29851704}. When further subclassification is not possible, the term “HPV-associated (or HPV-independent) adenocarcinoma NOS” is acceptable.

Tumour diathesis and tumour cells occur singly or in small, tight, 3D clusters or papillary configurations. Tumour cells with scant cytoplasm and intracytoplasmic neutrophils are common {31186178}. Uterine serous carcinoma frequently shows papillary clusters composed of large pleomorphic tumour cells with prominent nucleoli in a background of necrosis. Singles cells and bare nuclei can also be seen {15716611}.

Essential: confirmatory endometrioid features (primary or secondary endometrioid carcinoma); HPV negativity (primary or secondary endometrioid carcinoma, serous carcinoma, HPV-independent adenocarcinoma NOS); association of cervical endometriosis (primary or secondary endometrioid carcinoma); tumour should not involve uterine corpus or lower uterine segment (primary endometrioid or serous carcinoma); tumour should not involve uterine adnexa (secondary high-grade serous carcinoma).

Desirable: p16 and/or mRNA-based high-risk HPV in situ hybridization (to ascertain HPV-associated); p53 immunohistochemistry (for the serous carcinoma differential diagnosis).
Adenocarcinoma of the uterine cervix is staged as cervical carcinoma if primary.
The prognosis of primary endometrioid adenocarcinoma is unclear due to the previous lack of uniform criteria.
